data.venue: International Conference on Information Management and Engineering

data.abstract: Link prediction, as one of the core tasks of graph learning, aims to infer the potential connection relationships in the graph through the known topological structure. In recent years, the development direction of link prediction has gradually shifted towards causality and local structural performance. This paper proposes LinkMI-GNN - a link prediction model that integrates variational autoencoders, orthogonal decomposition of causal features and Gaussian mutual information enhancement. Based on the Gaussian hidden feature z output by the variational autoencoder, the causal feature c is extracted through orthogonal decomposition while keeping the Gaussian distribution characteristics unchanged. The Gaussian mutual information is utilized as the regularization term to enhance the causality of causal features. To improve the local structural performance of the entire model, the k-hop subgraph was added for link prediction. Experiments on the Cora and PubMed benchmark datasets showed that the AUC performance of LinkMI-GNN was 94.1% and 95.3% respectively.

data.abstract: Link prediction using graph neural network is a critical issue in the field of graph-structured data mining. While many models employ message passing based on rooted subtrees to aggregate the neighboring structure information surrounding the target nodes, leading to ignore the connection information among these nodes. Moreover, combining local structural features with message passing enhance the efficiency of link prediction but fails to effectively discerning common neighbors with varying features. To address the above challenges, a new model called Subgraph Sampling and Common Neighbors Fusion-based Graph Neural Networks for Link Prediction (SSCNF-GNN) is proposed. Specifically, we construct a subgraph by sampling neighboring nodes of the target node for message passing. To discern common neighbors’ distinct features while incorporating local structural features into MPNN for link prediction, their node representations are combined with those of the target nodes as a link predictor. Extensive experiments conducted on real datasets show that SSCNF-GNN outperforms baseline methods. Ablation experiments confirm the essential roles of message passing on subgraphs and capturing diverse common neighbor features as local structural features.

data.title: Demystifying Distributed Training of Graph Neural Networks for Link Prediction
data.venue: IEEE International Conference on Distributed Computing Systems

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20818, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are powerful tools for solving graph-related problems. Distributed GNN frameworks and systems enhance the scalability of GNNs and accelerate model training, yet most are optimized for node classification. Their performance on link prediction remains underexplored. This paper demystifies distributed training of GNNs for link prediction by investigating the issue of performance degradation when each worker trains a GNN on its assigned partitioned subgraph without having access to the entire graph. We discover that the main sources of the issue come from not only the information loss caused by graph partitioning but also the ways of drawing negative samples during model training. While sharing the complete graph information with each worker resolves the issue and preserves link prediction accuracy, it incurs a high communication cost. We propose SpLPG, which effectively leverages graph sparsification to mitigate the issue of performance degradation at a reduced communication cost. Experiment results on several public real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SpLPG, which reduces the communication overhead by up to about 80% while mostly preserving link prediction accuracy.

data.abstract: Recently, deep neural networks have revolutionized the field of link prediction, and the state-of-the-art works are typically subgraph-based discriminative methods, which construct features of local subgraphs firstly and predicting potential links via deep learning based binary subgraph classification. However, the discriminative link prediction methods always fail to automatically learn features and perform link prediction, and the performance of them depends on the construction of enclosing subgraphs and the manually-designed features for the subgraphs. To address these issues, we leverage the idea of graph disentangling and propose a novel self-representation-based generative graph neural network framework (GraphLP) for end-to-end link prediction, which learns to extract the latent patterns, i.e., recurring subgraphs, from input graphs via self-supervised learning and reconstruct graphs for link prediction using the subgraphs as structural basis. GraphLP consists of three components: self-representation-based collaborative inference, high-order connectivity computation, and multi-scale pattern fusion. The key idea is to utilize the correlations between the extracted recurring subgraphs on different scales to effectively assist link inference. GraphLP also can effectively exploit the hierarchical organization patterns and incorporate them within the representation procedure, producing robust and accurate results. Compared with traditional methods and state-of-the-art methods, experimental results on public benchmark datasets demonstrate that GraphLP achieves promising performance. Different from the discriminative methods, GraphLP provides a new paradigm for generative neural-network-based link prediction.

data.abstract: Link prediction is a crucial task in network analysis, widely used in areas like social network recommendation, knowledge graph completion, and bioinformatics. Traditional link prediction methods often rely on local structure or global embedding information of nodes, making it challenging to fully capture the complex node relationships. This paper introduces a link prediction method based on multi-feature fusion. The method combines Node2Vec, SEAL, and Graph Attention Network (GAT). Firstly, the Node2Vec algorithm is used to extract global features of nodes through random walks, capturing the network's global structural information. Then, the SEAL method extracts local structural features from the local subgraph of the target node pair, generating the local feature representation of the node pair through the subgraph embedding model. These global and local features are fused, and the fusion features are learned through GAT to predict potential network connection relationships more accurately by adaptively weighing the relationship weights between different nodes. Experimental results on multiple public datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing mainstream methods in link prediction tasks, particularly in evaluation indicators such as Hit@k and MRR. This method not only improves the accuracy of link prediction but also shows potential for application in large-scale complex networks, providing a new direction for link prediction research.

data.abstract: The Graph Neural Network (GNN) methods based on enclosing subgraph extraction have achieved excellent results in static graph link prediction tasks. However, most real-world networks are dynamic and evolve over time; the traditional models cannot capture temporal evolution. Moreover, the existing temporal link prediction methods mainly use simple GNNs to learn spatial embeddings, which not only ignore the higher-order relationships and local clustering structures between nodes, but also perform poorly in static graph link prediction tasks. In order to address the above problems, we propose Hypergraph Neural Networks for Temporal Link Prediction(HGTLP), which is based on enclosing subgraph extraction. The proposed HGTLP constructs a hypergraph through enclosing subgraph extraction and dual hypergraph transformation to learn the higher-order spatial and temporal embeddings of each link to be predicted, and then combines the global knowledge of the collapsed graph to improve the prediction accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that HGTLP achieves significant performance improvement compared to the state-of-the-art models in both link prediction and new link prediction tasks.

data.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven to be highly effective in addressing the link prediction problem. However, the need for large amounts of user data to learn representations of user interactions raises concerns about data privacy. While differential privacy (DP) techniques have been widely used for node-level tasks in graphs, incorporating DP into GNNs for link prediction is challenging due to data dependency. To this end, in this work we propose a differentially private link prediction (DPLP) framework, building upon subgraph-based GNNs. DPLP includes a DP-compliant subgraph extraction module as its core component. We first propose a neighborhood subgraph extraction method, and carefully analyze its data dependency level. To reduce this dependency, we optimize DPLP by integrating a novel path subgraph extraction method, which alleviates the utility loss in GNNs by reducing the noise sensitivity. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that our approaches achieve a good balance between privacy protection and prediction accuracy, even when using GNNs with few layers. We extensively evaluate our approaches on benchmark datasets and show that they can learn accurate privacy-preserving GNNs and outperforms the existing methods for link prediction.

data.title: GENIE: Watermarking Graph Neural Networks for Link Prediction

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.04805, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: The rapid adoption, usefulness, and resource-intensive training of Graph Neural Network (GNN) models have made them an invaluable intellectual property in graph-based machine learning. However, their wide-spread adoption also makes them susceptible to stealing, necessitating robust Ownership Demonstration (OD) techniques. Watermarking is a promising OD framework for deep neural networks, but existing methods fail to generalize to GNNs due to the non-Euclidean nature of graph data. Existing works on GNN watermarking primarily focus on node and graph classification, overlooking Link Prediction (LP). In this paper, we propose GENIE (watermarking Graph nEural Networks for lInk prEdiction), the first scheme to watermark GNNs for LP. GENIE creates a novel backdoor for both node-representation and subgraph-based LP methods, utilizing a unique trigger set and a secret watermark vector. Our OD scheme is equipped with Dynamic Watermark Thresholding (DWT), ensuring high verification probability while addressing practical issues in existing OD schemes. We extensively evaluate GENIE across 4 diverse model architectures (i.e., SEAL, GCN, GraphSAGE and NeoGNN), 7 real-world datasets and 21 watermark removal techniques and demonstrate its robustness to watermark removal and ownership piracy attacks. Finally, we discuss adaptive attacks against GENIE and a defense strategy to counter it. The codebase and related artifacts are publicly available at our Project Page.

data.title: Subgraph-Aware Graph Kernel Neural Network for Link Prediction in Biological Networks
data.venue: IEEE journal of biomedical and health informatics

openAccessPdf.disclaimer: Notice: Paper or abstract available at https://api.unpaywall.org/v2/10.1109/JBHI.2024.3390092?email=<INSERT_YOUR_EMAIL> or https://doi.org/10.1109/JBHI.2024.3390092, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

data.abstract: Identifying links within biological networks is important in various biomedical applications. Recent studies have revealed that each node in a network may play a unique role in different links, but most link prediction methods overlook distinctive node roles, hindering the acquisition of effective link representations. Subgraph-based methods have been introduced as solutions but often ignore shared information among subgraphs. To address these limitations, we propose a Subgraph-aware Graph Kernel Neural Network (SubKNet) for link prediction in biological networks. Specifically, SubKNet extracts a subgraph for each node pair and feeds it into a graph kernel neural network, which decomposes each subgraph into a combination of trainable graph filters with diversity regularization for subgraph-aware representation learning. Additionally, node embeddings of the network are extracted as auxiliary information, aiding in distinguishing node pairs that share the same subgraph. Extensive experiments on five biological networks demonstrate that SubKNet outperforms baselines, including methods especially designed for biological networks and methods adapted to various networks. Further investigations confirm that employing graph filters to subgraphs helps to distinguish node roles in different subgraphs, and the inclusion of diversity regularization further enhances its capacity from diverse perspectives, generating effective link representations that contribute to more accurate link prediction.

data.venue: International Conference on Parallel and Distributed Systems

data.abstract: Recently, the link prediction methods based on enclosing subgraph extraction and line graph transformation have been proven to achieve excellent prediction accuracy, but there are still some shortcomings, for examples, the time and space complexity of line graph transformation is too high and the graph neural network it used ignores the high-order relationship and local clustering structure between nodes, which makes it difficult to be widely used in real life and may affect the prediction accuracy. To solve the above problems, a hypergraph neural network model based on enclosing subgraph extraction is proposed, which converts subgraph into hypergraph by dual hypergraph transformation, and uses the hypergraph convolutional neural network to learn the higher-order features of nodes and edges respectively. After three experiments, the results show that the proposed model not only has higher prediction accuracy, but also has shorter runtime and less memory usage.
